concept.name: Procedural memory
concept.definition: An agent's store of 'how-to' knowledge: the rules, routines, and skills that govern how it acts — in language agents, implemented as a mixture of the model's trained weights, system prompts, code, and tool-use procedures. In the CoALA framework this contrasts with declarative stores (episodic and semantic memory) that record what, not how.
concept.intuition: The agent's habits and training manual: not facts or events, but the procedures it follows — like 'always verify contract specs before sizing a trade'.
concept.mechanics: Procedural knowledge lives in model parameters (learned skills), in explicit instructions (system prompts, playbooks, checklists), and in executable code or workflows the agent invokes. Unlike episodic/semantic memory, it is rarely written at runtime; updating it means editing prompts/code or retraining/fine-tuning.
concept.failure_modes: Flawed procedures execute reliably and repeatedly — a bad checklist is applied consistently every time. Because procedural memory is split across weights, prompts, and code, updates to one layer can be silently contradicted by another.
concept.misconceptions: Procedural memory is not just 'instructions in the prompt' — much of it is baked into model weights and cannot be inspected or edited directly. Adding more rules does not guarantee compliance; enforcement belongs in code outside the model where possible.
concept.example: A trading agent's procedural memory includes the rule 'before citing a statistic, retrieve it from the knowledge library rather than recall it', enforced partly by prompt instructions and partly by the orchestration code that routes such queries to retrieval.

citations.source: Sumers et al., 'Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)' (2023)
